title: Talk People Out of a New Role Before Talking Them Into It
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Argues leaders should flip the standard recruiting pitch by laying out a new role's hardships and downsides candidly before selling its upside, rather than the reverse. The reasoning is that overselling creates an implicit promise that reality inevitably breaks, leaving new hires feeling duped and demotivated once they encounter the actual difficulty of the job. By front-loading the negatives and then pivoting to genuine conviction about why the person will succeed anyway, leaders produce hires who arrive with realistic expectations, are less likely to sour early, and often find the role better than advertised.
points: Overselling a role creates implicit promises that reality inevitably breaks, leaving new hires feeling mugged by the gap between pitch and experience.
Leading with the role's genuine hardships before pivoting to conviction about why the candidate will succeed produces hires who arrive with realistic expectations.
Candor about downsides doesn't repel talented candidates -- it builds the trust that makes the eventual positive pitch land as credible rather than sales talk.
quotes: Once the candidate is “sold” and they show up to operate in the new role, they often find matters are very different from what they expected.
Not surprisingly, they sometimes feel mugged by the reality they walked into and duped by the leader who convinced them to accept the role.
That’s why smart leaders flip the normal script for persuasion. They talk people out of the job or role before talking them into it.
They choose to be brutally honest about what could go wrong and why it might not work out. They get specific about the downsides and negatives to the role.
Talented people appreciate this honesty. More importantly, once they show up, they arrive with realistic expectations and a more complete picture of the situation.
All because they weren’t sold a false reality. Now that’s a pretty picture.
